blocks.text: Function of two variables
UNIT IV: FUNCTIONS OF SEVERAL VARIABLES
If for all \(x,y\) a unique value \(f(x,y)\) is associated then \(f\) is said to be a function of two independent variables \(x\) & \(y\). It is denoted with
Partial derivative
A partial derivative of a function of several variables is the ordinary derivative w.r.t one of the variable when all the remaining variables are kept constant.

The partial derivation of the function \(v=f(x,y)\) is the ordinary derivative w.r.t \(x\) when \(y\) is kept constant. It is denoted with \(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}\) (or) \(v_x\) and is defined as
\[v_x=\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}=\lim_{\Delta x\to0}\dfrac{v(x+\Delta x,y)-v(x,y)}{\Delta x}\]
Similarly
\[v_y=\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}=\lim_{\Delta y\to0}\dfrac{v(x,y+\Delta y)-v(x,y)}{\Delta y}\]
The above partial derivatives are called first order derivatives.
Second order and mixed partial derivatives
The second order partial derivatives can be written as
\[v_{xx}=\dfrac{\partial^2v}{\partial x^2}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}\right)\]
\[v_{yy}=\dfrac{\partial^2v}{\partial y^2}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\]
\[v_{xy}=\dfrac{\partial^2v}{\partial x\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\]
\[v_{yx}=\dfrac{\partial^2v}{\partial y\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}\right)\]

pages.heading: Total Derivatives and the Chain Rule

blocks.text: Total Derivative (or) Total differential coefficient
Let \(z=\phi(x,y)\) be a function of 2 variables where \(x=f(t),\ y=g(t)\) then
\[\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial t}=\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\dfrac{dx}{dt}+\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\dfrac{dy}{dt}\]
is called the total derivative of the function \(z=\phi(x,y)\)
we can write \(dz=\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}dx+\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}dy\) this is called total differential coefficient.
The chain rule of partial differentiation
If \(z=\phi(u,v)\) where \(u=f(x,y),\ v=g(x,y)\) then
\[\text{i)}\quad\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u}\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v}\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}\]
\[\text{ii)}\quad\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u}\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v}\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}\]
The partial derivatives are called the chain rule of partial differentiation.
Similarly we can extend the above formula w.r.t 3 functions w.r.t 3 variables.

items.title: Total derivative — logarithmic and exponential substitution
question_paragraphs: Q. If the function \(u=x^2y^3\) where \(x=\log t\) & \(y=e^t\) then find \(\dfrac{du}{dt}\).
paragraphs: Sol:- By using total derivative formula we can write
\[\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}\dfrac{dx}{dt}+\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\dfrac{dy}{dt}\]
\[\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2y^3)=2xy^3,\quad\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2y^3)=3y^2x^2\]

items.title: Composite function — two partial derivatives
question_paragraphs: Q. If \(f=u^2v\) then \(u=e^{x^2-y^2},\ v=\sin(xy^2)\) find \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x},\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\).
paragraphs: Sol:- By using total derivative formula
\[\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial u}\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial v}\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}\]
\[\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial u}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}(u^2v)=2uv,\quad\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial v}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial v}(u^2v)=u^2\]
\[\text{ii)}\quad\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial u}\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial v}\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}\]

items.title: Chain-rule identity — linear substitutions
question_paragraphs: Q. \(w=f(2x-3y;3y-4z;4z-2x)\) then P.T \(6\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}+4\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y}+3\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z}=0\).
paragraphs: \[\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial t}{\partial x}\]
\[=\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}(2)+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}(0)+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}(-2)\]
\[\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}=2\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}-2\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}\quad\to(1)\]

\[\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial t}{\partial y}\]
\[=\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}(-3)+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}(3)+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}(0)\]
\[\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y}=-3\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}+3\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}\quad\to(2)\]

\[\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z}=\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial z}+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial z}+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial t}{\partial z}\]
\[=\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}(0)+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}(-4)+\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}(4)\]
\[\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z}=-4\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}+4\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}\quad\to(3)\]
\[\text{R.H.S}\to6\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x}+4\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y}+3\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z}\]

\[6\left[2\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}-2\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}\right]+4\left(-3\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}+3\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}\right)+3\left(-4\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial s}+4\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial t}\right)=0\]

items.title: Chain-rule identity — ratio substitutions
question_paragraphs: Q. If \(U=f(r,s,t),\ r=\dfrac{x}{y},\ s=\dfrac{y}{z},\ t=\dfrac{z}{x}\) P.T \(x\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial x}+y\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial y}+z\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial z}=0\).
paragraphs: \[\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial t}{\partial x}\]
\[=\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\left[\dfrac1y\right]+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}[0]+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\left[\dfrac{-z}{x^2}\right]\]

\[\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial t}{\partial z}\]

\[\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial z}=\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\dfrac{\partial r}{\partial z}+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial z}+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\dfrac{\partial t}{\partial z}\]
\[x\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial x}+y\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial y}+z\left(\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial z}\right)\]

\[=x\left[\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\left(\dfrac1y\right)-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\left(\dfrac{z}{x^2}\right)\right]+y\left[-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\left(\dfrac{x}{y^2}\right)+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}\left(\dfrac1z\right)\right]+z\left[-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}\left(\dfrac{y}{z^2}\right)+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\left(\dfrac1x\right)\right]\]

\[=\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\left(\dfrac{z}{x}\right)-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial r}\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}\left(\dfrac{y}{z}\right)-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial s}\left(\dfrac{y}{z}\right)+\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial t}\left(\dfrac{z}{x}\right)=0\]

blocks.text: Homogeneous Function
The function \(f(x,y)\) is said to be homogeneous if \(f(kx,ky)=k^nf(x,y)\) here ‘\(n\)’ is called the degree of the homogeneous function \(f(x,y)\).
If the function \(f(x,y)\) is trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic etc and \(f(x,y)\) is said to homogeneous function if
\[f(x,y)=x^n\phi\left(\dfrac yx\right)\]
\[f(x,y)=y^n\phi\left(\dfrac xy\right)\]
Euler’s Formula
If the function \(f(x,y)\) is homogeneous then
\[x\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}+y\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}=nf\]
\[x^2\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial x^2}+2xy\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial x\partial y}+y^2\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial y^2}=n(n-1)f\]
If the function is with three variables i.e. \(f(x,y,z)\)
\[x\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}+y\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}+z\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}=nf\]

items.title: Euler’s formula — tangent relation
question_paragraphs: Q. If \(\tan u=\dfrac{x^3+y^3}{x-y}\) P.T \(xu_x+yu_y=\sin2u\).
paragraphs: \[\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\tan u)=\sec^2u\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}\]
\[\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\tan u)=\sec^2u\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\]
\[(1)\Rightarrow x\left[\sec^2u\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right]+y\left[\sec^2u\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right]=2\tan u\]

blocks.text: Jacobian
Let \(u=u(x,y)\) and \(v=v(x,y)\) then these two simultaneous relations constitute a transformation from \((u,v)\) to \((x,y)\) i.e. the determinant
\[\begin{vmatrix}\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}&\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}\\\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}&\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}\end{vmatrix}\]
is called the Jacobian of the two functions \(u,v\) w.r.t the two variables \(x,y\). It is denoted with \(J\left(\dfrac{u,v}{x,y}\right)\) (or) \(\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\).
Similarly the Jacobian of the three functions \(u,v,w\) w.r.t the three variables \(x,y,z\) can be written as \(J\left(\dfrac{u,v,w}{x,y,z}\right)\) (or) \(\dfrac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}\)
\[(\text{or})\quad\begin{vmatrix}u_x&u_y&u_z\\v_x&v_y&v_z\\w_x&w_y&w_z\end{vmatrix}\]
Functionally Dependent and Independent
The two functions \(u=u(x,y)\) and \(v=v(x,y)\) are said to be functionally dependent if
\[J\left(\dfrac{u,v}{x,y}\right)=0\]
The two functions \(u,v\) are said to functionally independent if
\[J\left(\dfrac{u,v}{x,y}\right)\ne0\]
Properties of Jacobian
1) If \(u,v\) are the two functions w.r.t the two variables \(x,y\) then
\[\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\times\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=1\quad\Rightarrow JJ'=1\]
2) If \(u,v\) are functions of \(r,s\) and \(r,s\) are functions of \(x,y\) then
\[\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(r,s)}\times\dfrac{\partial(r,s)}{\partial(x,y)}\]

pages.heading: Taylor’s and Maclaurin’s Expansions

blocks.text: Tayler series of function of two variables
For the function of two variables \(x,y\) the tayler series expansion about the point \(x=a;\ y=b\) (or) in powers of \((x-a),(y-b)\) can be written as
\[f(x,y)=f(a,b)+\left\{(x-a)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}_{(a,b)}+(y-b)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}_{(a,b)}\right\}\]

\[+\dfrac1{2!}\left\{(x-a)^2\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial x^2}_{(a,b)}+2(x-a)(y-b)\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial x\partial y}_{(a,b)}+(y-b)^2\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial y^2}_{(a,b)}\right\}+\cdots\quad\to(1)\]
Eq (1) is called the tayler series expansion of \(f(x,y)\) about the point \((a,b)\).
Maclaurin’s series expansion
Put \(a=0,b=0\) in eq (1) we get

pages.heading: Maxima and Minima of Two-Variable Functions

blocks.text: Maximum, minimum, extreme and stationary values
Maximum and Minimum of functions of several variables

Let \(f(x,y)\) be a function of two variables and it is said to be a maximum value or minimum value at the point \(x=a,\ y=b\) if \(f(a,b)>f(a+h,b+k)\) (or) \(f(a,b)<f(a+h,b+k)\) where \(h,k\) are small values.
Extreme value: If \(f(a,b)\) is said to be an extreme value of the given function if it has maximum or minimum value.
Stationary value: If \(f(a,b)\) is said to be a stationary value of the given function if \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}_{(a,b)}=0\) and \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}_{(a,b)}=0\).
Note: Every extreme value is stationary value but converse need not be true.
Procedure to find maximum & minimum value
Procedure to find maximum & minimum value of \(f(x,y)\)
1. Find \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) and \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) and equate each to zero and solve these equations for \(x\) and \(y\).

2. Find \(\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial x^2}(=\ell),\ \dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial x\partial y}(=m)\) and \(\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial y^2}(=n)\). For each pair of values \((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2),\ldots\)
3. If i) \(\ell n-m^2>0,\ \ell<0\) at \((x_1,y_1)\) then the function has the maximum value at the point \((x_1,y_1)\).
ii) If \(\ell n-m^2>0\) and \(\ell>0\) at the point \((x_2,y_2)\) then the function has minimum value at the point \((x_2,y_2)\).
iii) If \(\ell n-m^2<0\) at the point \((x_3,y_3)\) then the function has neither maximum nor minimum.
iv) If \(\ell n-m^2=0\) then at any point then no conclusion can be drawn about maximum or minimum value of the given function. we require further investigation to find max or min value.

blocks.text: Lagrange’s Method of undetermined Multipliers
Suppose it is required to find the extreme of (max or min) for the function \(f(x,y,z)\) subject to the condition \(\phi(x,y,z)=0\) → (1)
Step 1: Form the Lagrange function
\[F(x,y,z)=f(x,y,z)+\lambda\phi(x,y,z)\]
Here \(\lambda\) is called the lagrangian multiplier which is determined by the following conditions.
Step 2:
\[\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x}=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}+\lambda\dfrac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}=0\quad\to(2)\]
\[\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}+\lambda\dfrac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}=0\quad\to(3)\]
\[\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial z}=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}+\lambda\dfrac{\partial\phi}{\partial z}=0\quad\to(4)\]

Step 3: Solve the equations from (1) – (4) for \(x,y,z\). The values of \(x,y\) and \(z\) are called the stationary points of the function \(f(x,y,z)\). Substitute \(x,y,z\) in the given function. It will give the maximum or minimum value of the function \(f(x,y,z)\).
Note: To find the extreme of \(f(x,y,z)\) w.r.t the conditions \(\phi(x,y,z)=0\) & \(\psi(x,y,z)=0\) then form the lagrangian function
\[F=f+\lambda\phi+\mu\psi\]
Here \(\lambda,\mu\) are called the lagrangian multipliers.
